note: The Economic Systems Lab is an open research programme for testing competing explanations. Its first model is ILLUSTRATIVE and uses SYNTHETIC household archetypes in currency-neutral units. Outputs are not forecasts, not calibrated to any country and not evidence about any policy.

researchQuestions.question: Why does economic growth not always translate into proportionate improvements in household security?
evidenceNeeds: Household budget surveys with essential-cost detail
researchQuestions.modelSupport: MODEL-HHR-01 illustrates the arithmetic channel; it does not test which explanation holds.

researchQuestions.question: How do wages, productivity, employment, housing costs and essential living costs interact for different household types?
evidenceNeeds: Price indices for essential goods by income group
researchQuestions.modelSupport: MODEL-HHR-01 makes these interactions explicit for synthetic archetypes.

researchQuestions.question: How do economic institutions and policies affect the distribution of opportunity?
Which mechanisms contribute to persistent economic insecurity?
evidenceNeeds: Panel data on income volatility and buffers
researchQuestions.modelSupport: MODEL-HHR-01 reports buffer months under deficits.

researchQuestions.question: How might AI-driven productivity change labour demand, income and wealth distribution?
evidenceNeeds: Evidence on hours and employment effects
researchQuestions.modelSupport: MODEL-HHR-01 includes exposure-weighted hours scenarios as assumptions, not predictions.

researchQuestions.question: What are the trade-offs, uncertainties and distributional consequences of alternative policy scenarios?
researchQuestions.modelSupport: Scenario comparison with one-at-a-time sensitivity in MODEL-HHR-01.

competingExplanations.explanation: Productivity gains are passed to pay only partially (institutions, bargaining power, market concentration).
competingExplanations.testableImplication: Pay growth below productivity growth after consistent deflation and compensation definitions.
competingExplanations.measurementCaveat: Measured gaps depend on deflators, compensation versus wages, and averages versus medians.

competingExplanations.explanation: Essential costs, especially housing and energy, rise faster than general prices for some households.
competingExplanations.testableImplication: Residual income after essentials falls for affected groups even when average real income rises.
competingExplanations.measurementCaveat: Requires group-specific price indices and housing-cost data.

competingExplanations.explanation: Growth is concentrated in sectors or regions where low-income households are not employed.
competingExplanations.testableImplication: Regional or sectoral divergence in earnings growth.
competingExplanations.measurementCaveat: Composition effects and migration can mislead.

competingExplanations.explanation: Hours and employment instability, not hourly pay, drive insecurity.
competingExplanations.testableImplication: Volatility of hours explains more variation in shortfalls than wage rates.

competingExplanations.explanation: Transfers are not indexed to the costs households face.
competingExplanations.testableImplication: Real value of transfers falls when essential costs rise.
competingExplanations.measurementCaveat: Indexation rules vary by programme and country.

models.title: Household residual-income resilience model
models.purpose: Make explicit how changes in wages, hours, employment, transfers and essential costs combine to change residual income for different household types.
formulas: gross earnings = Σ over earners (hourly wage × (1 + wage change) × monthly hours × (1 + hours change + automation hours change × automation exposure) × employment share)
wage change = nominal wage change + productivity growth × pass-through share
disposable income = gross earnings × (1 − effective tax and contribution rate) + transfers × (1 + transfer change)
essential costs = housing × (1 + housing change) + energy × (1 + energy change) + food × (1 + food change) + transport and other essentials × (1 + other change)
residual income = disposable income − essential costs
essentials share = essential costs ÷ disposable income (undefined when disposable income ≤ 0)
buffer months = savings ÷ (−residual income) when residual income is below zero; not depleting otherwise
status = deficit if residual is below zero; fragile if residual is below fragility threshold × disposable income; margin otherwise
assumptions: All archetype inputs are synthetic and currency-neutral; they are not calibrated to any country, survey or person.
Price changes pass fully into expenses; households do not ration or substitute (behavioural responses are excluded).
The effective tax and contribution rate is constant; transfers do not respond automatically to income changes.
Productivity growth affects pay only through the stated pass-through share; employment effects enter only through stated hours and employment changes.
Automation exposure is an illustrative multiplier applied only to the automation hours change, not an empirical exposure estimate.
The fragility threshold (default 10% of disposable income) is an analytical convention, not an official poverty line.
limitations: No general-equilibrium effects, prices or labour-market feedback.
No uncertainty quantification beyond deterministic one-at-a-time sensitivity.
Archetypes are not representative of any population; results cannot be aggregated into population statistics.
Cannot establish causal effects of any policy.
models.pathwayToAdvancedModels: Calibration to official household survey microdata, microsimulation of tax-benefit rules, and independent review are required before any empirical use.

scenarios.title: Baseline
scenarios.description: Synthetic starting values with no changes.

scenarios.title: Growth with low pass-through
scenarios.description: Productivity rises 10% but only 30% reaches pay; housing +8%, energy +5%, food +4%.

scenarios.title: Essential-cost shock
scenarios.description: Energy +40% and food +10% with no change in pay or transfers.

scenarios.title: AI productivity with hours displacement
scenarios.description: Productivity +15% with 50% pass-through; hours fall 10% scaled by each earner's illustrative automation exposure.

scenarios.title: Broad-based gains
scenarios.description: Productivity +10% with 90% pass-through; transfers indexed +3%; modest cost increases.

establishedDatasets.name: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform

No evidence claims are yet attached to the systems mechanisms M-ESSENTIAL-COSTS-OUTPACING-INCOME and M-PRODUCTIVITY-PAY-PASS-THROUGH.
